hero.headline.text: The model doesn't remember the last turn.

hero.highlight.text: The program sends the history again.

hero.takeaway.text: Every request stands alone. A multi-turn conversation works because the program puts the earlier messages back into messages. The longer the history, the bigger each request.

concepts.01-stateless.description.text: Nothing is kept between model calls. If something was said in the last request and is not in this one, the model doesn't know it.

concepts.02-history.description.text: Message history is a list the program holds. Each turn appends the question and the answer, and the next request sends the whole list again.

concepts.03-context.description.text: Context is everything in this one request. What is not in messages, the model cannot see.

concepts.04-cost.description.text: The whole history is resent every turn, so each request is bigger than the last. prompt_tokens in usage records the size of each one.

section-1.title.text: The model doesn't remember the last turn on its own

section-1.paragraphs.0.text: The model does not remember the last turn on its own. Every request is independent: if something was said in the last request and is not in this one, the model doesn't know it. {{lesson:chat-request}} sent only one request, so this problem didn't show. This lesson asks twice. In turn 1 you tell the model "I have a cat named Tuanzi", and in turn 2 you ask "What is my cat's name?". If the second request contains only the second question, the model has no way to know the name Tuanzi.

section-1.paragraphs.1.text: Yet the chat apps you have used clearly remember what you said earlier. That's because the app resends the earlier messages behind the scenes, and the model reads the whole conversation from the start every time. It is like writing to an adviser who keeps no copies: every letter has to attach all the earlier correspondence before he can pick up the thread.

section-1.paragraphs.2.text: Why doesn't the model side keep anything? A provider handles a huge number of requests at once, and each one is computed only from what it carries, then finished. The model's parameters are fixed after training, and no amount of chatting changes them. So the only facts the second request can use are the ones written in it.

section-1.paragraphs.3.text: Some providers offer an interface that saves the conversation for you, so you don't resend each time. In that case the provider stores the messages and splices them into the next request; the model itself still reads from the start every time, and the details are in the provider's documentation. The interface used in this lesson saves nothing. This lesson also calls no tools. It just lays out the act of resending history.

misconception-model-learns.claim.text: The chat app remembers what I said earlier, so the model must learn from the conversation and store what I said.

misconception-model-learns.correction.text: The model's parameters are fixed after training, and what you say does not change them. The app remembers because the program puts the earlier messages, or key points distilled from them, into this request. Take those messages out and the model doesn't know: the exercise "Ask a follow-up without history" in this lesson is the evidence.

section-2.title.text: Message history lives in the program

section-2.paragraphs.0.text: A multi-turn conversation depends on a list the program holds, the message history. In this lesson run keeps it in a Python list called history, which starts with one system message. Each turn first appends that turn's user question and then sends the request; once the answer arrives, it is appended too, as a message with role assistant. So by the next turn, history holds the previous turn's question and answer.

section-2.paragraphs.1.text: Take turn 2. The exercise "Ask a follow-up with history" sends four messages: system, the turn 1 user, the turn 1 assistant, and the turn 2 user. The exercise "Ask a follow-up without history" uses latest_only mode and sends only two: system and the turn 2 user. In this mode history still has each turn's question and answer appended; only the request takes just the first and the last entry. The two arms run the same code except for the one line that decides "what to send", so if the model can't give the name in turn 2, only that line can be the cause.

section-2.paragraphs.2.text: The answer has to be put back too, not just the question. In turn 3 you ask "How old is it this year?". What "it" refers to can only be known from the earlier conversation. And what the model said last turn must also be visible next turn, so that it doesn't contradict itself. On the lab bench you can check this word for word: in the arm with history, messages[2] of the turn 2 request is exactly the content of the turn 1 response.

section-2.paragraphs.3.text: history is just an ordinary Python list, and it lives only for this one run. When the run ends it is gone, and the next run starts again from a single system message. Run "Ask a follow-up with history" twice, and the first request of the second run has none of the messages from the first run. To keep things across runs, you have to write them to a file or database yourself; {{lesson:persistent-memory}} covers that. Claude Code works the same way. The official documentation says every new session starts with an empty context and carries no message history from earlier sessions. `claude --continue` can pick up the last conversation because it writes every message and tool result into a session file on your machine, reads them back on resume, and appends new messages after them.

deep-dive-history-rewrite.summary.text: The model cannot tell whether an assistant message in the history was really said by itself. It only goes by what this request says.

deep-dive-history-rewrite.paragraphs.0.text: When the turn 2 request reaches the provider, the four messages are joined into one block of text by the chat template described in {{lesson:chat-request}}, with a marker at the end that means "the assistant's turn to speak". The model reads from start to end and then continues. To it, turn 1's question and answer and turn 2's question are all just parts of that text.

deep-dive-history-rewrite.paragraphs.1.text: One consequence is that the model has no way to verify whether an assistant message in the history was really said by itself. For example: the program changes turn 1's answer from "Got it" to "OK, Tuanzi is five this year", then asks "How old is it this year?". What the model reads is that it "said" five, and it will very likely go along with it, even if the turn 1 user message said three. Which message is a real answer and which was edited by the program cannot be seen in the request.

deep-dive-history-rewrite.paragraphs.2.text: This is both a risk and a tool. The risk: if the history is recorded wrongly, the model uses the wrong thing as fact. The tool: the program can tidy the history on purpose, for example delete outdated messages or write a long stretch of conversation as a summary. The later lessons on context all do this.

deep-dive-history-rewrite.paragraphs.3.text: Beyond tidying, the program can also add content to the history: put in a few written example question-and-answer pairs first, and the model often follows the format and tone of the examples. Those examples were never said by the model. They are just text the program placed in the request, and the model still reads them as earlier conversation.

deep-dive-history-rewrite.paragraphs.4.text: In this lesson history is appended as is, with no entry changed. So the messages you see in the request event are what the model actually read this turn. To find out why the model answered as it did, look there first.

predict-request-count.prompt.text: Run it once first. In the experiment "With and without history", before you run "Ask a follow-up without history", guess: how many model requests (request events) will this run send?

mq-which-message.which-message.prompt.text: In the turn 2 request with history, which message lets the model know the cat is named Tuanzi?

mq-which-message.which-message.a.feedbac.text: Correct. The name is what you said in the turn 1 user message, and the program resent that message unchanged.

mq-which-message.which-message.b.text.text: The model remembered the last turn itself

mq-which-message.which-message.b.feedbac.text: Not quite. The model keeps no state between calls; if this message is not in the request, the model can't see it.

mq-which-message.which-message.c.feedbac.text: Not quite. system holds only the answering rules, and the cat's name is not in it.

mq-which-message.which-message.explanati.text: A fact the model can use has to be in messages of this one request.

section-3.title.text: Context: everything in this one request

section-3.paragraphs.0.text: Context is everything the model can see in this one request. In this lesson that means the messages in messages: the system rules, the question and answer of each earlier turn, and this turn's question. What is not in messages, the model cannot see. What is in it, the model can use, whichever turn it came from.

section-3.paragraphs.1.text: So "remembering" is really a choice the program makes: which messages go into this request. This lesson's latest_only mode puts in only system and this turn's question, so the fact from turn 1 is not in the context. Later lessons will also trim, summarize, or select from the history. They all do the same thing: decide what this request carries.

section-3.paragraphs.2.text: More context is not always better. A request can hold only so many tokens, and a provider usually returns an error when you exceed the limit. Even below the limit you still pay: after ten turns about the cat, if you ask about the weather, the earlier ten turns are still in the request and still cost money. With a lot of irrelevant content, the model may also overlook the important information. {{lesson:context-budget}} covers these. In the lessons on tools, the context will also include tool definitions and execution results, but the principle is the same: the model can only use what is in this request.

section-3.paragraphs.3.text: Knowledge the model learned in training is not context. It knows a cat is an animal because it saw a lot of text like that during training. It can know your cat is named Tuanzi only because this request says so. Telling the two sources apart lets you judge where an answer comes from: the first cannot be checked item by item, while the second you can check in the request event.

compare-second-turn.rows.0.1.text: system, turn 1 user, turn 1 assistant, turn 2 user

compare-second-turn.rows.1.1.text: Yes, in the turn 1 user message

compare-second-turn.rows.2.0.text: What the cat-name answer is based on

compare-second-turn.rows.2.2.text: Nothing in the request; the model can only say it doesn't know, or guess

section-4.title.text: The longer the history, the bigger each request

section-4.paragraphs.0.text: The whole history is resent every turn, so each request is bigger than the last. With the full history, turn 3 sends six messages: system, three user, and two assistant. Each extra turn adds two messages to the request. prompt_tokens in usage records the prompt tokens of all the messages in this request, and it grows turn by turn.

section-4.paragraphs.1.text: A made-up example: system is 20 tokens, each question 15, each answer 20. Turn 1's prompt tokens are `20 + 15 = 35`. Turn 2 adds turn 1's answer and the new question, so `35 + 20 + 15 = 70`. Turn 3 is 105. The user asks just one more sentence each turn, yet the prompt tokens grow by 35 each turn.

section-4.paragraphs.2.text: Every request is billed on the whole history, so the longer you chat, the more each turn costs. The lab report for the exercise "Three-turn conversation" lists prompt_tokens for each turn. Compare the difference between adjacent turns and see whether it is close to the previous turn's answer plus this turn's question. The markers the provider adds when joining messages are counted too, so the difference is a little more than the text alone. How much it actually grows is for your own run to show.

section-4.paragraphs.3.text: In two cases the growth differs from the calculation above. One is a reasoning model: this lesson puts only the answer's content back into the history, not the reasoning, so completion_tokens may be large while the next turn's prompt_tokens grows only by that answer and the new question. The other is sending only this turn's question: the prompt tokens stay roughly flat each turn and change only slightly with the length of the question. The tokens that arm saves are exactly the history, which is why it can't answer the cat's name.

deep-dive-cost-growth.title.text: By hand: how many tokens ten turns send in total

deep-dive-cost-growth.summary.text: Each turn's request grows linearly with the turn number, so adding up ten or twenty turns gives a total that grows close to quadratically.

deep-dive-cost-growth.paragraphs.0.text: Use the made-up numbers from the text again: system 20, each question 15, each answer 20. Each extra turn adds 35 prompt tokens, so turn 10 is `35 × 10 = 350`, ten times turn 1.

deep-dive-cost-growth.paragraphs.1.text: And ten turns added up? `35 + 70 + … + 350 = 35 × 55 = 1925`. If each turn sent only system and that turn's question, ten turns would total `35 × 10 = 350`. Resending the history makes the total prompt tokens over ten turns 5.5 times as large. Doubling to 20 turns gives `35 × 210 = 7350`, about 4 times the 10-turn total: each turn's request grows linearly with the turn number, so the total grows close to quadratically.

deep-dive-cost-growth.paragraphs.2.text: This doesn't yet count answers that get longer or users pasting in big blocks of text. In real long conversations, prompt tokens quickly take most of the total, and completion tokens are the small part. So later lessons do two things. One is to control how much history each request carries: {{lesson:context-budget}} and {{lesson:context-compaction}} cover trimming and summarizing. The other is to make the repeated part cheaper: some providers charge less for the part that matches the start of the previous request, which {{lesson:prompt-caching}} covers. Claude Code's cost documentation describes the same accounting: every request carries the full conversation, so a short question in a session that has been open all day is still billed on the whole conversation. One approach the documentation gives is to start a new session with `/clear` when you switch to an unrelated task.

deep-dive-cost-growth.paragraphs.3.text: When doing this arithmetic, use only the numbers usage reports. The numbers above are made up. The real growth is whatever your "Three-turn conversation" lab report shows. When the provider does not report a number, the report shows "not reported", and you can't fill it in with the formula here.

mq-growth.why-growth.prompt.text: In the three-turn conversation, turn 3 has more prompt_tokens than turn 1. What is the main reason?

mq-growth.why-growth.a.text.text: The turn 3 request carries the questions and answers of the first two turns

mq-growth.why-growth.a.feedback.text: Correct. Prompt tokens are counted over all the messages sent this time, so the longer the history, the more there are.

mq-growth.why-growth.b.text.text: The model thought more in turn 3

mq-growth.why-growth.b.feedback.text: Not quite. What the model writes is counted in completion_tokens. prompt_tokens counts only the messages sent.

mq-growth.why-growth.c.text.text: The provider charges more by turn number

mq-growth.why-growth.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The provider doesn't know which turn this is. It computes only from the content of this one request.

mq-growth.why-growth.explanation.text: Each request is computed independently. The program resends the history every turn.

section-5.title.text: The program decides which history to carry

section-5.paragraphs.0.text: Which history to carry and how to arrange it is entirely up to the program. The model just reads this one request. This lesson's two modes are the two simplest choices: send the whole history, or send only system and this turn's question. With the first, the model can follow the conversation but requests keep growing. With the second, requests are smallest but the model can't follow.

section-5.paragraphs.1.text: Real applications sit between the two. The program can keep only the last few turns, write the earlier conversation as a summary, or pick only the few messages relevant to the current question. For example, a support conversation might keep the last five turns plus a one-line summary, "the user is asking about returning order 12345". However you choose, keep two rules: put questions and answers back in pairs, and keep the order intact. Otherwise the model reads a conversation with its head cut off and tends to answer off the point.

section-5.paragraphs.2.text: {{lesson:sampling-variance}} will also show that sending the same request again can give a different answer. The answer you put back into the history is just one such result, and the following turns all continue from it. By {{lesson:tool-selection}}, history will also hold the calls the model proposed and the tools' execution results, and the program still appends them one by one and sends the whole thing.

section-5.paragraphs.3.text: When reading a multi-turn run, don't look only at the last answer. First check which messages the last request carried, then judge whether the answer had a basis. If the answer gets the cat's name right but "Tuanzi" was never in the request, that was luck. If it was in the request and the answer is wrong, the model failed to use it. Keep the two cases apart.

mq-pairs.pairs-in-history.prompt.text: The program wants to keep only the most recent messages. Which way of deleting leaves the model reading a conversation with its head cut off?

mq-pairs.pairs-in-history.a.text.text: Keep the turn 2 assistant answer but delete the user question before it

mq-pairs.pairs-in-history.a.feedback.text: Correct. The answer has lost its question, so the model doesn't know what it is answering.

mq-pairs.pairs-in-history.b.text.text: Delete turn 1's question and answer; keep system and turn 2's question and answer

mq-pairs.pairs-in-history.b.feedback.text: Not quite. A complete question-and-answer pair was deleted, and the rest of the conversation is still paired and in order.

mq-pairs.pairs-in-history.c.text.text: Delete nothing and send the whole history

mq-pairs.pairs-in-history.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The whole history is complete; the request is just larger.

mq-pairs.pairs-in-history.explanation.text: When trimming history, keep questions and answers in pairs and keep the order.

code-turns.n9.text.text: The three turns' questions are hard-coded here. Turns 2 and 3 can only be answered with the fact from turn 1, which is what makes the effect of carrying or not carrying history visible.

code-loop.n20.text.text: The two modes differ in one place: whether each turn sends the whole history or only system and this turn's question.

code-loop.n21.text.text: At most three turns. max_rounds in lesson.json is also 3, so one more request would be blocked by the platform.

code-loop.n27.text.text: Take the runtime text for this run's language: the system prompt, the three questions and the report texts all come from t.

code-loop.n37.text.text: The message history is this ordinary Python list. When the run ends it is gone, and the next run starts from scratch.

code-loop.n39.text.text: One request per turn. number is passed to the platform as round_number, and the timeline groups by it.

code-loop.n41.text.text: The first append: this turn's question.

code-loop.n43.text.text: This line decides what the model can see this time. latest_only mode takes only the first message (system) and the last one (user).

code-loop.n44.text.text: context.complete copies the request body before recording it, so appending to history afterward does not change the request event already recorded.

code-loop.n48.text.text: The second append: the model's answer. latest_only mode appends it too; it just isn't sent next turn.

code-loop.n50.text.text: The last turn's answer is the final answer of this run.

code-loop.fold-record.label.text: Platform: record the messages and response actually sent this turn, for the lab report

code-decision.title.text: History lives in the program's list and is resent in full each turn

code-decision.chosen.text: run keeps each turn's user question and assistant answer in the history list itself, and every request puts the complete set of messages to send into messages. The model side keeps nothing, and whatever was sent is recorded in the request event.

code-decision.provider-session.title.text: Let the provider store the session

code-decision.provider-session.why_not.text: The interface used in this lesson does not store sessions. Even where a provider offers a session feature, which history was actually used each time is no longer laid out in the request, so you can't check it item by item.

code-decision.latest-only.title.text: Send only the latest turn's question

code-decision.latest-only.why_not.text: It saves prompt tokens, but the model can't see the facts said earlier. That is exactly the "Ask a follow-up without history" arm.

history-or-not.hypothesis.text: Turn 1 is identical in both arms. When turn 2 carries turn 1's question and answer, the cat's name is in the request and the model can answer from it. When only the second question is sent, the name is not in the request and the model has no way to answer.

history-or-not.first-request.text.text: messages of the turn 1 request: both arms have system and the turn 1 user, exactly the same.

history-or-not.second-request.text.text: messages of the turn 2 request: the arm with history has four, and the arm without history has only two.

history-or-not.second-answer.text.text: The answer in the turn 2 response: see whether it states the cat's name.

history-or-not.checks.text.text: The lab report's checks: whether the turn 2 request contains turn 1's fact, and whether the answer mentions it.

history-or-not.guide.0.text.text: This run sent two requests. Look at turn 1 first; the two arms don't differ here.

history-or-not.guide.1.text.text: The cat's name is in the turn 1 user message.

history-or-not.guide.2.text.text: Count how many messages turn 2 sent, and look for "Tuanzi" in them.

history-or-not.guide.3.text.text: The model can only answer from the messages in this one request.

history-or-not.guide.4.text.text: The first check looks at the messages sent, and the second looks at the answer. Only with the former does the latter mean anything.

history-or-not.conclusion.proves.0.text: Which messages turn 2 actually sent in this run, and whether turn 1's fact is among them.

history-or-not.conclusion.proves.1.text: Without history, the model had already "heard" the name in turn 1 and still can't get it in turn 2: the previous call left nothing behind.

history-or-not.conclusion.does_not_prove.text: That the arm with history answered correctly only shows the basis was in the request. It doesn't guarantee the model will use it correctly every time.
The wording of an answer varies from run to run; sending the same request again can also give a different answer.

growing-history.hypothesis.text: Asking three turns with the whole history, each request has two more messages than the last, and prompt_tokens grows turn by turn.

growing-history.third-request.text.text: messages of the turn 3 request: six messages, with the questions and answers of both earlier turns in it.

growing-history.third-usage.text.text: usage.prompt_tokens of the turn 3 response: the prompt tokens of all the messages in this request.

growing-history.per-turn.text.text: The lab report's table: the number of messages sent each turn and prompt_tokens. Items that were not reported show "not reported".

growing-history.guide.0.text.text: This run asked three turns. First see how long the last request is.

growing-history.guide.1.text.text: Turn 3's question is a single sentence, but the request carries all the questions and answers from the first two turns.

growing-history.guide.2.text.text: The provider counts prompt tokens over all the messages in this one request.

growing-history.guide.3.text.text: Read the prompt tokens column from top to bottom, then work out how much adjacent turns differ.

growing-history.conclusion.proves.0.text: The number of messages actually sent each turn in this run, and the prompt tokens per turn that the provider reported.

growing-history.conclusion.proves.1.text: The growth in prompt tokens comes from the resent history: each turn's request contains all the earlier questions and answers.

growing-history.conclusion.does_not_prov.text: How much it grows per turn depends on the length of the answers and the provider's tokenizer, and the numbers will differ on another model.
Three turns can't tell you what happens after dozens of turns. When the history gets too long it needs trimming or summarizing, which later lessons cover.

quiz.who-remembers.prompt.text: In a multi-turn conversation, who does the "remembering" of what was said last turn?

quiz.who-remembers.a.text.text: The program: it puts the earlier messages into the next request

quiz.who-remembers.a.feedback.text: Correct. The program holds the message history and puts the messages to send into messages each turn.

quiz.who-remembers.b.text.text: The model: it remembers what the same user said

quiz.who-remembers.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The model keeps no state between calls, and the arm without history is the evidence.

quiz.who-remembers.c.text.text: The provider: it saves the session by API key

quiz.who-remembers.c.feedback.text: Not quite. The interface in this lesson does not save sessions; each request is handled only by its own content.

quiz.who-remembers.explanation.text: "Remembering" means the program decides which messages this request carries.

quiz.assistant-back.prompt.text: What happens if the program puts only each turn's user question back into history and not the assistant answer?

quiz.assistant-back.a.text.text: In the next turn the model can't see what it said in the last turn

quiz.assistant-back.a.feedback.text: Correct. If the answer isn't in the request, the model doesn't know what it answered.

quiz.assistant-back.b.text.text: No effect; the model fills in the last turn's answer itself

quiz.assistant-back.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The model sees only the messages in this request and does not fill in what wasn't sent.

quiz.assistant-back.c.text.text: The request errors because the assistant message is missing

quiz.assistant-back.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Most providers accept several user messages in a row, and the request succeeds. It just lacks the model's own answers.

quiz.assistant-back.explanation.text: Put both questions and answers back so the next turn's context is complete.

quiz.context-means.prompt.text: In this lesson, what is the model's context in the turn 2 request?

quiz.context-means.a.text.text: All the messages in messages of the turn 2 request

quiz.context-means.a.feedback.text: Correct. Context is everything in this one request.

quiz.context-means.b.text.text: All the requests this run has sent

quiz.context-means.b.feedback.text: Not quite. The turn 1 request is already over. The model sees only what was put back into the turn 2 messages.

quiz.context-means.c.text.text: All the text the model saw in training

quiz.context-means.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Training data affects how the model answers, but the cat's name you gave this time can only come from the request.

quiz.context-means.explanation.text: The program reassembles the context for every request.

quiz.growth-calc.prompt.text: A made-up example: system is 20 tokens, each question 15, each answer 20. With the full history, roughly how many prompt tokens does the turn 3 request have?

quiz.growth-calc.a.text.text: 105: system, three questions, and two answers

quiz.growth-calc.a.feedback.text: Correct. `20 + 15 × 3 + 20 × 2 = 105`, and each extra turn adds 35.

quiz.growth-calc.b.feedback.text: Not quite. That is the size when only this turn's question is sent. With history, the first two turns' questions and answers are in the request too.

quiz.growth-calc.c.feedback.text: Not quite. Turn 3's answer hasn't been written yet and is not in this request.

quiz.growth-calc.explanation.text: Prompt tokens are counted over all the messages in this request, and every extra turn of history adds one question and one answer.

check-hunt.prompt.text: Run "Three-turn conversation" and find the request where the model first gets to see the turn 2 answer.

check-hunt.explanation.text: It is the turn 3 request: messages[4] is the turn 2 assistant answer. The program appends it to history after turn 2 ends, and only then is turn 3 sent. The turn 2 request doesn't have it yet.
